newsitem.title: USA: Finance officials set to launch aid plan for poor.
newsitem.headline: Finance officials set to launch aid plan for poor.

text.p: By Rich Miller, U.S. Economics Correspondent
Top finance officials were set on Monday to formally launch a multi-billion-dollar debt relief plan for the world's poorest countries that has been years in the making.

The programme, which would involve action by creditor countries, the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, is designed to relieve up to $7.7 billion of debts of as many as 20 poor nations, most of them in Africa.

The joint Development Committee of the IMF and World Bank was expected to endorse the proposal at its meeting on Monday, paving the way for the nitty-gritty work to begin on which countries will benefit first, and how much. A decision on that is expected by the end of the year.

Among those likely to be first in line, according to British officials, are Uganda, the Ivory Coast, Ethiopia and Guyana. Other possible beneficiaries include Bolivia, Mali and Burkina Faso, they said.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Sunday he expected the new debt relief initiative to prove as important for poor countries as the 1989 Brady plan was for middle income developing nations.

That debt-reduction plan, named after former U.S. Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady, proved to be just the elixir that many countries in Latin America needed to restore their economies to full health.

"There is now a real opportunity to bring down the curtain on the debt crisis in the world's poorest countries," said Justin Forsyth, representative of the environmental and development group Oxfam International. "The challenge now is to move rapidly towards implementation."
In deciding to formally launch the debt initiative on Monday, finance officials are leaving open a number of questions about its financing that will ultimately have to be dealt with.
The IMF's policy-making Interim Committee pledged on Monday to find the money it needs to participate in the plan, but stopped short of spelling out where it would come from.

The decision, announced in a communique issued after a day of talks, effectively left unanswered the question of whether the IMF will eventually sell off some of its gold to finance stepped-up aid for the world's poor.
IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus, backed up by the United States and most of the Fund's member nations, has proposed selling up to five million ounces of gold.
But a handful of other nations, particularly Germany, are opposed, and instead want the IMF to use contributions from its member nations to finance the increased aid.
Also unanswered is the question of where the cash-strapped African Development Bank, which is also supposed to participate in the plan, will find the money to take part. REUTER
